# 03. Same-Day Client Check-ins

Source: 8/24/2026 GPC <> Rush check-in with Lacy Buckingham Robertson and Marcelo Maceira, held after the four interviews. Citation tag **[check-in]** unless noted.

This call converts a day of interviews into client confidence. It ran about 41 minutes and followed a consistent shape.

## The shape of the call

1. **Recap the day in the client's favor.** Open by praising what their people gave you: "wow, this is a treasure trove of ideas." The sponsors chose these interviewees, so make them look right for it. **Read the correction in the next section before repeating any numbers from this recap.**
2. **Connect what you saw to the strategic thread.** Jesse's self-built agents became the live case study for the governance conversation Jason wants: individual builds a tool, value proves out, then it hardens to enterprise grade. Grant's framing on the call: "when you build that, it needs to have a path to make its way to bubble up to the surface, multiple people are getting use and value from it. And then it gets to enterprise level security." Interviews aren't just data collection, they're evidence for the strategy you're already forming.
3. **Answer the client's process questions with your actual method.** Marcelo asked whether their opportunity intake form is best practice. Grant gave the layered answer (business-case sizing, constraint focus, business-goal focus) and validated their instinct while adding the interview-plus-survey layer: "is it a best practice to get information from the team? Yes, that's exactly what we're doing. But we're going through interviews and on top of survey." Teach on the call. It's free consulting that compounds trust.
4. **Confirm the political calendar.** Lacy corrected the sequence in the room: the board meeting comes after the leadership conference, not before. Deliverable dates then got negotiated backward from the event: workflow mapping readout in about three weeks, mid-September; outline review Monday the 14th; review with Jody on the 16th or 17th, which Grant sized as "48 hours to get that cleaned up before we present to Jody." Deadlines exist to protect the sponsor's standing with their executive.
5. **Demo the work in progress and take the hit.** See below.
6. **Convert the day's findings into demo candidates on the spot.** The RGM carve-out pain (named files: 2026-0824 New DSA and Corp AR 071326, both captured on the Peterbilt call hours earlier **[peterbilt]**) became the proposed demo within minutes of the interviews ending. "Show me my region's impact in this sheet in the things that I need to make decisions on" was chosen because it is, in Grant's words, "as determinist as we can get," it maps to recorded evidence, and every RGM benefits even though Jody doesn't touch it directly.
7. **End with owned action items.** Survey memo to Lacy, an email written in Jody's voice by Grant for the sponsors to touch up, file requests going to Justin and Hal with Lacy on CC, and a Claude access check after the call. Every item has an owner and most have a date.

## Correction: the warranty numbers

This one is in the playbook because getting it wrong is the point.

Jesse's actual claim, made live on his own screen share: the warranty agent has been in use for two months, "it's cut down on our kickbacks by 30%, and has also helped increase what we're able to claim by an additional 17%." **[gm-1]** So: kickbacks down 30 percent, claimable amount up 17 percent.

On the check-in a few hours later, Grant repeated it as "we've increased warranty revenue or the clawbacks by 17% and reduced the time spent by 30%," and flagged his own uncertainty in the same breath: "I don't know where those numbers are from, but they sure sound good." **[check-in]** The 17 percent survived, the 30 percent changed meaning from rejected claims to time spent.

The same drift shows up earlier in the day. Hal described a $60,000 gross profit hit at the Long Beach store from a mispriced bucket of oil, and Grant summarized it back a minute later as "this $65,000 oil expense." **[peterbilt]**

The operating rule: capture client numbers verbatim in the moment, and re-read them before repeating them to a sponsor. A number said back wrong to the person who owns the report is a credibility cost that a whole day of good interviews has to pay for. Earlier drafts of this playbook carried Grant's version of Jesse's numbers rather than Jesse's; the corrected version is above.

A counter-instance from 8/25, for balance: Chad's "We were missing 20,000 customer calls a month for one segment of our business" came back later in the same call as "the priority comes from the fact that you guys are missing 20,000 calls" — exact. **[aftermarket]** (tag defined in module 00). The drift risk is highest when a number crosses calls and hours, not minutes; the same-day sponsor recap is the danger zone, which is what this module's rule is for.

## The demo-feedback moment (study this one)

Olivia demoed the reworked Jody asset. Lacy's feedback was blunt: better format, wrong report, possibly not worth doing at all ("is this, like, even a worthy one to work on?"). What happened next is the move to learn:

- **Nobody defended the asset.** Olivia agreed in real time ("this is not the right report") and widened the aperture ("We also don't have to go at it with just one specific prompt or one specific sheet. If there's a few different sheets you want to throw at me to see if maybe we can get [there]").
- **Grant named the real constraint without blaming anyone.** One transcript of Jody working, one easy spreadsheet, no email access: "And I know it's nobody's... It's just the constraints of what we're dealing with." He then stated the dependency plainly: "when we know what the input is, we know what the spreadsheet is, and we know what the output is or what you're looking to learn, we can help." Then the ask, framed as "transcript plus asset equals knowledge."
- **The sponsors took on part of the input problem themselves.** Lacy offered to coach the executive toward a harder example ("I need you to think about something that is more complex that you're comfortable pairing two different reports against each other... if you could walk Grant and Olivia through that specifically on a call"), and Marcelo named the root cause without defensiveness: "there's no lack of reports to analyze. It just so happens that Jody picked the easiest one to give you guys." Killing your own demo gracefully is what buys that help.
- **The group problem-solved forward.** Within about ten minutes the dead-end Jody demo became a stronger candidate (the RGM carve-out) plus a plan to get Grant into, or a recording out of, the Monday truck sales BUGM call. BUGM is the client's own acronym for their business unit growth metrics review; Marcelo supplied the expansion on the call and the transcript renders the spoken form as "buggums."

The lesson: a demo that gets killed on a check-in call is a success if it dies fast and something better gets chosen in the same meeting. The failure mode is defending weak work or iterating on it over email for a week.

## Managing the nervous executive

The sponsors are anxious about Jody and say so. Lacy: "I just am nervous that Jody's going to, he's going to be putting like the pressure on. Do you think we can hold him off until that week?" Marcelo: "Is there any way we could get something... something light that we can get him ahead in terms of direction of what's happening. Just because it's a new endeavor, and he's nervous." The GO call adds the earlier read that the COO "was not impressed by the first tutoring session" **[go]**. Describing him as skeptical rather than nervous is a reading of that, not a quote **[inferred]**.

The handling pattern:

- Give the sponsor something light and early ("a little nibble for him": the demo now, a one or two page findings note mid-next week) rather than making them hold the line until the big readout.
- Write in the executive's voice for him to tweak ("I'll write the email from Jody's perspective, effectively saying this is what we're doing... You guys touch it up, you know, the way he likes to write"), and commit that it won't read as machine-written: "I will make sure it doesn't sound like AI."
- Ask the sponsors directly what they need: "whatever you need from us to help ease the process, we're a new partner for you... just say the word. It's not a burden for us whatsoever."
- Accept that you may not get executive time at all, and design around it. Marcelo: "we're not going to get enough of Jody's time to say, show me, I want to watch you analyze this spreadsheet. I don't think we're going to get that hour with him." The response was to find a recorded or attendable meeting where he works out loud instead of asking him for a session.
